p: The phrase cold war is the coinage, I learn, of the English writer George Orwell, the author of a grim fable called Nineteen Eighty-Four, though others gave it currency. It describes the long contest, from about nineteen forty-seven to nineteen ninety-one, between the United States of America and its allies on the one side and the Soviet Union and its allies on the other: a contest fought by every means short of direct war between the two great powers, because direct war, with atomic weapons, would have destroyed them both.

At the end of the Second World War, the Soviet armies stood in the middle of Europe, and the Soviet Union imposed communist governments upon the countries of the east: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria and the eastern part of Germany. Mr Churchill, speaking in Missouri in nineteen forty-six, said that an iron curtain had descended across the continent. The Americans, alarmed, pledged to support free peoples resisting subjugation, and gave enormous sums, under a plan named for their Secretary of State, George Marshall, to rebuild the shattered economies of Western Europe. In nineteen forty-nine, the Western nations formed an alliance, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, and the Soviets, in nineteen fifty-five, an alliance of their own. Germany was divided in two, and its old capital, Berlin, deep in the Soviet zone, was itself divided; in nineteen sixty-one the eastern government built a wall across the city to stop its people from fleeing to the west. Families on either side of a street were divided for twenty-eight years.

In nineteen forty-nine, the communists under Mao Zedong won the civil war in China. The Soviet Union exploded its own atomic bomb the same year, and within a few years both sides possessed the hydrogen bomb, a thousand times more powerful than the bomb of Hiroshima, and rockets that could carry it across the world in half an hour. The doctrine on which the peace of the world then rested was called, with an aptness that a Gibbon would have relished, mutually assured destruction, whose initials spell the English word mad.
## The wars that were not cold

The contest was cold only between the great powers themselves. Elsewhere it was very hot. In Korea, from nineteen fifty to fifty-three, and in Vietnam, from the nineteen-fifties to nineteen seventy-five, the Americans fought long wars against communist forces backed by the Soviet Union and China, at the cost of millions of lives. In Africa, Asia and Latin America, as the European empires dissolved after the war, India gaining its independence from Britain in nineteen forty-seven and most of Africa in the decade after nineteen fifty-seven, the two powers competed for the allegiance of the new nations by aid, by arms and by subversion.

The closest approach to the final catastrophe came in October nineteen sixty-two, when the Americans discovered that the Soviets were placing nuclear rockets on the island of Cuba, ninety miles from Florida. For thirteen days President John Kennedy and the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev stood, in the phrase of the time, eyeball to eyeball, and the world waited. A secret bargain resolved it. The Encyclopaedia records several later occasions on which the machines of warning mistakenly reported an attack, and the world was saved by individual officers who chose to disbelieve them. I do not find that reassuring.

The rockets which could carry bombs across the world could also carry machines and men beyond it. On the fourth of October, nineteen fifty-seven, the Soviet Union launched into orbit around the earth a polished metal sphere the size of a large ball, with four long aerials, called Sputnik, meaning fellow traveller, which went round the earth every ninety-six minutes, sending out a radio signal that anyone with a receiver could hear. The Americans were dismayed. In nineteen sixty-one, a young Soviet airman named Yuri Gagarin became the first human being to travel into space and round the earth, in a flight of an hour and forty-eight minutes. The American President Kennedy responded by declaring that his nation would land a man on the moon and return him safely to the earth before the decade was out.

They did. On the twentieth of July, nineteen sixty-nine, two Americans, Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin, landed on the moon in a small craft called the Eagle, while their companion Michael Collins circled overhead. As Armstrong stepped down, he said: that's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind. Some six hundred million people, the Encyclopaedia estimates, watched it at the same moment by means of a machine called television, which transmits moving pictures through the air. Twelve men in all walked upon the moon, the last in December nineteen seventy-two. None has been since.

The French romancer Mr Jules Verne, whose novel From the Earth to the Moon appeared ten years ago, imagined that men would be fired to the moon from a great cannon in Florida. The Americans launched from Florida. That is the kind of detail that makes a historian distrust his own sense of what is impossible.

The Cold War ended not in fire but in exhaustion. The Soviet economy, rigidly planned from the centre, could not match the productivity of the West, and its people knew it. In nineteen eighty-five a new Soviet leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, tried to reform the system by allowing greater openness. The openness undid it. In nineteen eighty-nine, the peoples of Eastern Europe overthrew their communist governments, mostly without bloodshed, and on the night of the ninth of November the people of Berlin began to tear down the wall with hammers. In December nineteen ninety-one, the Soviet Union itself dissolved into fifteen separate states.
Some Americans declared it the end of history. The historians of the future have been more cautious, and so shall I. History, in my experience, does not end. It merely changes the subject.
